thread.title: What Amazon's move tells us about the culture wars

author: morningstar.com
title: What Amazon's move tells us about the culture wars
text:
By Tim Mullaney
Successful companies want everything the Trump base isn't: educated, urban, diverse workforce
When Amazon.com unveiled its list of 20 finalists (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/amazon-releases-its-hq2-shortlist-and-this-is-what-weve-learned-from-it-2018-01-18)for its HQ2 satellite headquarters, whose 50,000 promised jobs have been making economic-development pros across North America drool, one thing was overlooked among the flood of initial commentary.
Not one finalist site was in a county President Donald Trump carried in 2016.
Not. One.
And that tells you something important about the culture wars, and how they're reflected in elections and eventually in policy and generational power -- and the economy. Trump and the cohort he has chosen, if only because they chose him first, are on the losing side.
Much was made after the election of the fact that the president won all but about 500 (https://www.factcheck.org/2016/12/clinton-counties/)of the nation's 3,141 counties, a fact made less impressive by knowledge that New Jersey, with 8.9 million people, has 21 counties, and Kansas, with 3 million, has 105. The counter was a study by the nonpartisan Brookings Institution that said counties voting against Trump generate 64% of America's gross domestic product (https://www.brookings.edu/blog/the-avenue/2016/11/29/another-clinton-trump-divide-high-output-america-vs-low-output-america/)-- a function of their much higher population density, incomes and educational levels.
Amazon's (AMZN) list is what that split looks like when important decisions come down to business, rather than politics.
Even in "red" states Trump carried, he got whomped in places where Amazon is actually looking. In Ohio, where Trump's 8.6-point win reversed two Democratic triumphs when Barack Obama was running, Trump commanded only 35% of the vote in Franklin County, where Columbus is.
In Georgia, Amazon's looking at Atlanta, where Trump got 27%. In North Carolina, Wake County (Raleigh) gave him 38%. He got 36% in Marion County, Ind., where the sitting governor in Indianapolis was Mike Pence, Trump's running mate.
And, et tu Texas? Trump got 27% in Travis County, where Austin is -- not unexpected since the local-business promotional slogan is "Keep Austin Weird." But the really funny part was watching Trump command less than 35% in Dallas County -- which is, y'know, Dallas.
So, not only did he lose everywhere Amazon is interested in going -- Trump got killed every place Amazon is looking, even in states he won.
It's not complicated, when you look at Amazon's criteria, to see why this would happen.
The list is dominated by code words for what, in a political context, you would see as modern liberalism, but to Amazon are just business. Great universities nearby, strong mass transit, a diverse population, and a "cultural fit," all in a metro area of at least 1 million people.
Which Wichita, the biggest metro entirely in Kansas, misses by a third.
In other words, Amazon had the same criteria that a biotech venture capitalist named Jim Barrett was thinking of 25 years ago, when he explained to me why bids from South Carolina and West Virginia to lure famed AIDS researcher Robert Gallo's lab from Washington's suburbs were nothing for Maryland economic-development officials to worry about.
Gallo isn't going, Barrett said decades before the rise of Trump, because he can't get his people to move to either of those places. And he was right.
This won't change because nothing about the future -- of the economy or American society -- supports the notion that ignorance is bliss. That idea is solely for political consumption.
People who are dubious about evolution still send their kids to college -- nearly 70% of high school grads at least start higher education (https://www.bls.gov/news.release/hsgec.nr0.htm). The kids don't emerge believing in climate denialism and creationism -- the habits of mind that higher education teaches rule that out. They don't think gays eat people or that transgenderism is a scam to let sex-offender wannabes hang out in bathrooms.
They certainly won't cast a man who pays off porn actresses as their defender of family values.
They will come out with 66% better lifetime earnings (https://trends.collegeboard.org/education-pays/figures-tables/lifetime-earnings-education-level)prospects, according to the Census Bureau. And that means parents will send them -- even if 58% of Republicans and GOP-leaning independents tell pollsters higher education is bad for America (http://www.pewresearch.org/fact-tank/2017/07/20/republicans-skeptical-of-colleges-impact-on-u-s-but-most-see-benefits-for-workforce-preparation/). Only a handful of dingbats actually believe that when it's their own kids' futures at stake.
In other words, the kids will graduate thinking, and acting, like Amazon. It's an easy prediction that Apple's (AAPL) search for a new alt-headquarters (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/apple-to-invest-350-billion-in-us-economy-and-create-20000-jobs-2018-01-17)outside Silicon Valley will turn out the same way. To make it in a brain-powered world, companies can't turn off their brains, or move to places where that's the political fashion.
An election can change that power dynamic for a term, or even two. But the economic power of the no-longer-new New Class isn't a voting mechanism -- it's a weighing mechanism. And it turns out that big heads weigh a lot, especially when they're not buried in sand.
-Tim Mullaney; 1010ET
